China is a highly interconnected society where the distance between people is minimal, posing significant challenges in managing contagious diseases. Unfortunately, a series of severe outbreaks in late 2019 and early 2020 led to widespread public anxiety and a loss of trust in official information, fostering the rapid dissemination of rumors on new media platforms. To understand the extent of rumor spread, this study focuses on measuring its influence in China during the COVID-19 pandemic. By collecting and cleaning up newly reported news from major Chinese online portals, a multi-label classification model was created to accurately identify rumor content. To capture the dynamic nature of influence spread, this study employs an SIRA model and measures indicator values using entropy-based methods. The results indicate that the most active users on Weibo who shared rumors were predominantly male, young, and located in the Yangtze River Delta region, often reposting content from official accounts without adding comments. In contrast, WeChat users, often motivated by emotional responses, tended to share the content with friends and family within their own circles, leading to limited scope of the spread. Consequently, managing the pandemic required not only timely and accurate government communication but also a strategic use of new media to promote official information and mitigate the negative effects of rumors.

Arid regions of the universe, such as the Fornax cluster, are ideal locations for astronomers to observe galaxies being shaped by a process known as quenching. This is primarily shaped by a global event called "starvation", caused by a lack of fuel for ongoing star formation, as well as more localized phenomena like "strangulation", which halts the flow of fuel, often in the form of hot gas, toward a galaxy's central area. Understanding the detailed processes of star formation in galaxies within the Fornax cluster is complicated, in part, by the presence of nebulae, such as supernovae remnants and gas clouds, that can confuse telescope observations. To better quench these chaotic regions, researchers need to develop better methods for analyzing the movements and compositions of gases within a galaxy, often called "kinematics and spectroscopy", to understand how the quenching processes are affecting the nebulae. 

To address these challenges, the Fornax3D project team is conducting a detailed study of several planetary nebulae within the Fornax cluster, spanning from 1919 to 1971, to map the movements and compositions of these small but significant celestial objects. By analyzing the planetary nebulae, the team will be able to more accurately measure the distances between several galaxies within the cluster, such as NGC 1614, NGC 1672, and NGC 1650, as well as

Google App Engine's Flexible Environment provides a platform for developing and deploying applications as Cloud Functions, with a limited set of available programming languages including Go, Java, Python, and Node.js. However, these applications are constrained to executing with a maximum timeout of 60 seconds, rendering them incapable of handling time-series data that requires real-time reallocation of resources every few seconds. To address this limitation, we present LifeStream, an in-memory flow processing framework designed to handle periodic data flows and dynamically reallocate resources every couple of seconds. LifeStream features dynamic scope trees for efficient memory allocation, parallelized event-driven computation, and the integration of user-defined algorithms with a limited set of basic functions. The framework is extensible with additional libraries, supports seamless migration of applications to and from Cloud Functions, with an added cost of only 0.01 USD at runtime. The performance of LifeStream is demonstrated through the implementation of resource reallocation, data transformation, and aggregation operations, with results showing runtimes up to 1000 times faster than the alternative of re-running applications, and 10 times faster than Streamlit.

This research paper focuses on identifying and discussing specific types of curves, namely Bertrand curves, as well as a subcategory, the Bertrand-Parietti curves, within a specific mathematical framework, the timelike Minkowski metric space R^3_1. We within this space define and discuss both the Bertrand and Bertrand-Parietti curves, and specifically how the latter arises within a certain mathematical framework.

The choice of loss function for a neural network is widely regarded as essential, yet this choice is often made with little consideration, and many standard functions are applied without thorough testing. Some research suggests that novel loss functions can significantly enhance performance, though this claim seems exaggerated. This study reevaluates the importance of loss functions by examining a broad spectrum of them across multiple deep learning architectures, datasets, and problem types for the classification task. We systematically tested more than 30 commonly used and novel loss functions, employing them in conjunction with established optimizer functions. Our experiments were conducted on four classification problems, using well-known benchmark datasets and diverse neural network models. We opted against introducing new loss functions to ensure a fair comparison. Our results indicate that, despite the variety of available functions, their impact on performance is surprisingly limited. In most cases, the standard cross-entropy loss matches or surpasses the accuracy of other tested losses.

A simple boundary feedback controller has been designed for stabilizing the solutions of the Navier-Stokes equations using a linear controller applied to a boundary that is not perpendicular. Building on previous work, the current study utilizes a more practical controller and leverages established results from nonlinear analysis to achieve local exponential stability. Moreover, the project extends to achieving asymptotic stability by modifying the controller, as demonstrated using a Lyapunov function approach.

This research employs a comprehensive thermomechanical model coupled with an Abbe's principle-based method to analyze the mechanical behavior of materials undergoing strain-induced crystallization (SIC). Abbe's method, although simple, provides an effective approximation of material response in areas experiencing significant large deformations. While typically associated with finite elasticity theory and material stabilization, Abbe's method has seen limited application in the context of SIC. To overcome this challenge, we modified Abbe's method by integrating Abbe's stress and Abbe's power with the rate of deformation and introduced a new material stabilization procedure. Furthermore, we investigated the impact of the synthesis rate of crystalline structure on Abbe's stress, Abbe's power, and Abbe's modulus of stiffness. The results from our simulations revealed that the strain-induced crystallization material can undergo substantial stiffening due to the rapid formation of crystalline structure, thus enabling the use of Abbe's method even in highly nonlinear scenarios.

To analyze the impact of spin interactions and magnetic sensitivity of the superconducting state, a nelemic Eliashberg theory is developed for near-doping critical cuprate materials, it involves deriving precise formulas for key superconducting parameters including the transition temperature, gap form factors, and magnetic susceptibility. The proposed framework is then applied to investigate the properties of triplet nematic superconducting state within the LMO system. The results obtained from this model indicate the existence of a stable state of superconductivity, characterized by a nematic order parameter that exists within a specific range, the susceptibility formula derived from this model demonstrates a quadratic relationship with the nematic order parameter, the model also predicts that the magnetic field can cause the superconducting state to transition into a paramagnetic state, the competition between these two states is modeled and the model's predictions are consistent with available experimental data.

External actors can effectively guide an agent's generalization and update its model based on the feedback they provide, which can be considered as updates in the confidence level rather than absolute knowledge. This paper presents an algorithm that enables a robotic agent to generalize and adapt from training data and learn from externally driven input when performing a task. Furthermore, this formulation is applicable to a broader range of settings, including situation-dependent feedback from external actors and internally generated states. We utilize a robust meta-algorithm to execute these externally generated inputs using state-space models and partially observable Markov decision processes. Additionally, we utilize summary statistics rather than explicit state observations, thereby facilitating the efficient use of computational resources.

Difference Carrier Phase (DCP) detection methods are vulnerable to an increased delay enhancement, specifically in differential detection, where a certain multiplier will cause the effective dispersion to be reduced. In the context of continuous phase modulation (CPM) detection, this strategy is found to be ineffective. We investigate the possibility of improving differential CPM detection techniques by evaluating various schemes, such as simple differential detection, decision-aided differential detection, and decision-aided raised cosine differential detection. We evaluate and compare these methods in terms of performance, complexity, and robustness against delays, and find that decision-aided differential detection and decision-aided raised cosine differential detection are decision-aided differential detection and decision-aided raised cosine differential detection offer superior immunity to delay perturbations.

The detection of gravitational waves from merging black holes and neutrons stars has previously been assumed to produce visible electromagnetic signals. However, recent research reveals that certain collapse dynamics during core-collapse supernovae can inhibit this connection. To assess the impact of quark matter on the possibility of identifying merging black hole-neutron star as electromagnetic sources, we employed numerical simulations to analyze the late-stage dynamics of supernovae, focusing on neutron star Todorov instability. Our findings indicate that increasing the density dependence of strong interactions reduces the likelihood of observing black hole-neutron star mergers that were previously estimated. Furthermore, density-driven effects on electromagnetic source candidates can result in a factor of 10 discrepancy between two previous estimates.

A previously reported finding indicates that the space-timeCompressibility, first explored by Steif in 1991, is closely associated with a quantum spacetime capacity, initially examined by Strocchi in 1977. This relationship was initially proven for scenarios where the Compressibility and Quantum Capacity are measured using the same type of perturbation, limiting its general applicability. Now, we generalize this connection to include cases where the measurements differ, specifically proving that the quantum spacetimeCompressibility is proportional to the square root of a squared difference between the fluctuations, which includes the previously discussed scenario as a subset. This proportionality factor is the sum of the thermal sources' masses, specifically demonstrated for a two-level system in a thermal state, where the sources are weighted by the probability of the system transitioning from an excited state to a lower energy level.

Having experienced heavy rainfall, distinguishing between a clear, rain-free day and a cloudy, rainy one can be quite challenging. Recent advancements in deep learning have enabled the easy creation of realistic images depicting both clear and rainy conditions. Conversely, accurately controlling the natural phenomenon of rain, as seen in real environments, remains a difficult task. Moreover, most generated rain often lacks the physical characteristics and visual effects typically associated with it. To overcome this limitation, we introduce a novel, unified framework capable of automatically transforming natural scenes into both rainy and non-rainy versions of themselves. Our Disentangled Translation Model learns the relationship between clouds and rain by separating the two elements. It first disentangles the input image into its respective components, then independently recreates rain or removes it using realistic physics-based techniques. As a result, our model produces highly photorealistic images featuring both realistic rain and distortion effects. Experimental evaluations demonstrate the proposed model's superior performance, significantly outperforming existing methods in both translation and enhancement tasks. For visual comparisons, see the supplementary video or our demo website.

The primary challenge in my autonomous driving system is to accurately identify positive and negative turns of maneuvers based on short video clips, a task that's also a typical cluster ranking problem. To tackle this, I've designed a simple but effective method called Visually Aided Cluster Ranking (VACR), which incorporates regularizing effects from visual features to constrain parameters and reduce the burden on labeled data. Furthermore, I've discovered that employing cluster-level features along with help from image predictions significantly enhances performance and substantially speeds up training when leveraging common optimizers like stochastic gradient descent, enabling rapid development of efficient reward models.

We examine how model-partial data models affect the continuous map preservation property, offering proof that these models inevitably lead to this property's preservation property. This proof holds for any dimension $d \geq 1$. Next, we investigate a specific scenario where the space is one-dimensional ($d=1$) and both models satisfy certain technical requirements. In this case, we establish that sequence models have the fixed point property, a outcome that has significant implications for the continuum problem in topology.

Q-curvature related issues on a fixed, finite area will significantly affect the underlying domain's characteristics, and this effect has been observed and studied in various forms, including those found in Q-curvature brane models, and a higher-order Brezis-Nirenberg type problem on a bounded domain has a similar connection.

In this work, we examine a Q-curvature problem with a specific constraint that includes both a cubic growth term and a lower-bounded term, and we establish the existence of non-trivial solutions for a given parameter where the bounded domain exhibits a conformal flat structure, and a compact manifold without such a structure. Additionally, we identify conditions under which the problem has a non-trivial solution for a sufficiently small parameter, and we have the relevant reference studies for further reference.

Assessing drug consumption risk in the medical field is a critical aspect of the treatment process. 
An important study on personality traits and their connection to drug consumption risk remains missing, 
which is why this research proposes using the Five Factor Model (FFM) to assess the stability 
of patients undergoing treatment for substance-related disorders. 
We tested the suitability of FFM for this purpose with structure-equation methods and a sample 
of 250 individuals, consisting of 100 drug consumers, 100 alcohol users, and 100 non-addicts. 
Analyzing FFM traits through latent variables and their individual facets, we found that an 
equation based on FFM traits achieved better results in predicting substance consumption risk 
than using traditional diagnostic methods. 
Notably, neuroticism played a key role in forming this risk assessment. 
We suggest employing an add-on module based on FFM to evaluate the consumption risk of alcohol 
and drugs within the medical field.

Despite recent breakthroughs, artificial intelligence systems still fall short of humans in their ability to adapt and apply logical reasoning, a skill essential for navigating intricate real-world situations. ATOMIC is an open-source framework composed of three components that investigate Structured Representations, Module Design, and Logical Rules within the context of Knowledge Graphs. ATOMIC leverages modern machine learning techniques to create a comprehensive atlas of structured representations that facilitate if-then reasoning. It focuses on two key aspects: linking predicted entities with their descriptions and categorizing entities within the graph. For module design, ATOMIC utilizes machine learning models that leverage external knowledge resources. It also explores the use of logical rules to enhance machine predictions. ATOMIC's analysis of structured representations, module efficiency, and the synergistic potential of data-driven and symbolic approaches within the context of knowledge graphs.

The HHL algorithm is a renowned quantum method for resolving linear systems of equations. Nevertheless, its application in financial sectors is hindered by: 1) the necessity of inputting the coefficient matrix $A$ into the algorithm, which is often infeasible for large-scale systems commonly encountered in the financial sector, and 2) the absence of verification for the accuracy of the obtained solution. To tackle these obstacles, we introduce NISQ-HHL, a novel adaptation of the HHL algorithm tailored for financial applications. This adaptation leverages the characteristics of the target system and employs iterative methods to achieve the following objectives: a) circumvent the imposition on $A$ by directly taking the right-hand side vector $b$ as the input, and b) facilitate portfolio checks, thereby providing a means for portfolio validation. We test NISQ-HHL on portfolio optimization and the development of error-corrected quantum algorithms. This study demonstrates that NISQ-HHL yields a high-quality, verifiable solution within a timeframe feasible for practical application, and it is also capable of generating solutions that can withstand the effects of quantum error correction codes.

To enhance data efficiency of state-of-the-art end-to-end ASR models and enable them to handle sufficient training with limited resource languages, a multi-modal training approach is proposed. This method involves leveraging both audio and text data. We further introduce two novel cross-modal attention mechanisms to capture the relevant text information for each audio data point and vice versa. These attention mechanisms are designed to establish a focus between the two modalities. Our proposed model integrates these bidirectional attention modules into the transformer-based ASR architecture. We observe that they are effective without compromising the model's overall training process. As an additional benefit, the proposed attention mechanisms can serve as a substitute for character-level modeling, thereby reducing the reliance on large-scale text data. Our work demonstrates significant improvement in word error rate by 4.17% on the Librispeech development set.

Inspired by a recent finding linking cross-section fluctuations to an invisible dimension, we investigated the connection between cross-section fluctuations and an additional dimension in more detail. To gain deeper insights, we carried out an extensive analysis of mixed correlations in proton-proton collisions at a energy of 13.6 TeV, using a vast dataset consisting of 37.7 trillion events. Our analysis revealed distinct regions in the parameter space where the fluctuation of the cross-section around its mean value takes on unexpectedly large values. To further explore, we investigated whether these significant fluctuation regions display characteristic properties predicted by the fractal hypothesis.

This paper investigates the long-term behavior of a randomly generated uniform parking distribution of size $n$, denoted as $\pi_n$. We establish that the first $k_n$ positions of $\pi_n$, $\pi_n(1)$ through $\pi_n(k_n)$, are asymptotically independent and identically distributed with a uniform probability distribution over the set $\{1, 2, \dots, n\}$ for two different distance metrics: total variation and Kolmogorov-Smirnov. Furthermore, we derive asymptotic rates of convergence, along with related stochastic process connections, to better understand the behavior of parking distributions.

Researchers investigated the electrical properties of superconducting nanowires made of Niobium nitride, demonstrating that adding a gate electrode can induce a transition from normal to superconducting state. A critical parameter in this transition is the normal state resistance of the nanowires, with higher resistance requiring a lower gate voltage to initiate the transition. A theoretical model based on coherent quantum phase slips provides an accurate prediction for this gate-controlled conduction phenomenon.

The T-dwarf star GJ 229B, which orbits as a brown dwarf companion to a main-sequence star, exhibits a unique atmospheric phenomenon. Discovered in 1995 as the first T-dwarf in our galaxy, GJ 229B also has a well-studied orbit, providing it with 18 Earth days of varying solar exposure. Although small, it still experiences temperature fluctuations due to its star, which may help us better understand how we shape our own atmosphere and the potential habitability of exoplanets. GJ 229B's atmospheric composition has been observed through various spectroscopic analyses, but the results have been difficult to interpret due to the effects of clouds on the spectrum. In this study, we present a comprehensive model of GJ 229B's atmosphere that accounts for its clouds and is constrained by a wide range of spectral observations, from visible to submillimeter wavelengths. Our model reveals a rich atmospheric composition, characterized by alternating layers of silicon dioxide haze and rich in molecular gases such as carbon monoxide, carbon dioxide, methane, and ammonia. We also find that these observations may be explained by an alternative model, in which tall upwellings and steep temperature gradients in the atmosphere of GJ 229B create a carbon-chain polymer haze similar to Jupiter's atmosphere, without requiring a specific type of haze known as SO$_2$.

Our study investigates the impact of virtual V-A current correlations on the quark-gluon medium, resulting in distinct structure functions that reveal insights into its internal composition. Through numerical calculations, we navigate the complete range of nucleon structure variables, d, to assess our findings, incorporating the influence of quark interactions, quantum chromodynamic corrections, and the quark-nucleon color pre-resonance, while drawing comparisons with established EPSK04 quark-gluon saturation data. To execute this investigation, we employ an on-line, state-of-the-art quark-gluon fluid model, grounded in relativistic hydrodynamics, to track the evolution and properties of the quark-gluon medium.

Building predictive models for camera angles in the context of immersive video is a critical challenge due to limited labeled data and the intricate nature of viewpoint estimation. To tackle this problem, conventional approaches rely on neural networks that process angular representations such as spherical coordinates or Euler angles. Unfortunately, these methods struggle with continuity and lead to suboptimal performance. To address these shortcomings, we propose a novel framework that utilizes dual vector representation and generative adversarial network to generate realistic video sequences from predicted camera angles. Our model achieves state-of-the-art results on the challenging NYU-V2 dataset, outperforming existing methods in terms of video prediction quality and camera angle estimation accuracy.

In a recent experiment, researchers applied intense ultrashort laser pulses in the terahertz range to a special type of semiconductor called GaAs quantum well. This allowed them to monitor how electrons at different energy levels interact with one another using time-resolved spectroscopy. They discovered that the strong laser pulses caused the separation between these energy levels to change, which then affected the transfer of energy between them. This study provides evidence for the intricate inter-level coupling phenomenon, a concept that has been difficult to demonstrate and has significant implications for our understanding of light-matter interactions.

The $\Omega^{-}$ baryon, containing three charm quarks, has recently been detected. Analyzing it allows researchers to understand how heavy quarks combine, with the goal of extending this study to a pair of $\chi_{c1}$ quarks and a $s$-quark. Using the QCD light-front wavefunction and consistent with the conventional QCD wavefunction approach, we calculate the mass spectrum and wavefunctions for this type of baryon. By applying the constituent quark model, our results for the masses of $\Omega^{-}$ and related baryons were verified against available data.

Airborne infections spread easily in enclosed spaces like bus interiors, especially during peak hours. To simulate the propagation of resvirola on a specific bus line, we applied a contact cable, considering features of the disease and settings that influence its transmission. Our analysis shows that the busirola peak occurred in late May 2020 and was most intense in May and June 2020, with the disease peak in late May 2020.

Building on my previous birefringence paper's findings, this report proposes concrete experiments to detect the effects of photon scattering off quantum vacuum fluctuations, specifically transverse momentum and polarization changes. While my earlier findings can be adapted for the proposed experiments, the primary and distinct content of this report lies in detailing suitable detection methods for quantum vacuum birefringence.

This note outlines the method used by Eisenlohr and Farris to determine the transitivity class of any fully invariant polyhedron $\mathcal{P}$ under the action of a group $G$. Their method involves first identifying the blocks of $G$ that are contained within the polyhedron $\mathcal{P}$, and then applying the action-to-map principle to assess the orbit transitivity of any subaction related to these blocks.

The concept of uncloneable encryption, initially explored by Boyar et al. and revitalized by Brakerski and Segev, revolves around creating an encryption method for classical bits that becomes ineffective once an adversary attempts to encrypt the same data with a different key. This preliminary work presents an enhanced version of the original schemes, achieving significant efficiency gains while reducing assumptions by utilizing a random oracle and only requiring a one-way function. Furthermore, it examines the link between uncloneable encryption and cloneless verification, a newly introduced idea for a cloning-resistant verification protocol.

Physical layer security is an emerging keyless authentication method, with
extractable shared secrets arising naturally between legitimate devices, derived
from unique hardware imperfections. This paper presents initial findings on
implementing keyless authentication in audio processing systems, applicable to
telecommunication networks. We explore whether a reliable and secure extraction
of a shared secret between two legitimate devices is possible in audio systems.
In contrast to previous studies focusing on encryption-based extraction, our
research investigates the occurrence of unique and shared characteristics
within audio processing systems. These findings are evaluated through the
KASQC protocol, demonstrating the potential for hardware-imperfection-derived
shared secrets in audio processing systems.

We utilized the full tight-binding model and random phase approximation to
explore flat-band plasmons in hole-doped twisted bilayer molybdenum disulfide.
Our calculations showed that lattice relaxation influences plasmon behavior.
When we considered intraband transitions, low-damped, flat plasmons emerged,
while accounting for interband transitions led to plasmon dispersion following
$\sqrt q$ law. The plasmon energies in these materials can be adjusted through
tweaking the twist angles and doping levels. For samples without lattice
relaxations, coexistence of low and high-energy plasmons occurs. Higher doping
levels however eliminate the quasi-flat plasmon. These observations imply that
two conditions must be satisfied: a flat band isolated from the other bands
and adequate doping level to witness the quasi-flat plasmon. The study offers
clues for exploring superconductivity mediated by plasmons in these materials.

This research paper establishes a connection between almost conformal gradient Ricci solitons and conformal gradient Ricci solitons, then applies this to Sasakian manifolds. We derive the structure of these solitons when they reside on such manifolds, and demonstrate that if a conformal Ricci soliton's potential vector field is also a conformal Killing vector field, it implies that the underlying Sasakian manifold possesses a constant scalar curvature. A new property of almost conformal gradient Ricci solitons is identified, and a relationship is discovered between this property and conformal Ricci solitons in Sasakian manifolds. Furthermore, we obtain a consequence of constant scalar curvature in projective hyperspherical manifolds.

Stars and planets experience mass loss due to winds shaped into magnetospheres by magnetic fields. The extent of these magnetic fields is determined by the balance between plasma carried by the wind and the star's magnetic field, which can be understood through the interaction length and standoff distance. Both systems consist of wind plasma, magnetic fields embedded in that plasma, and any present particles accelerated to high energies. However, stars and planets differ significantly due to their central bodies having varying properties, which affect their magnetic fields. For instance, planetary magnetic fields can interact with incoming stellar winds, creating magnetospheres that contain radiation belts. Additionally, some planets experience the deposition of wind energy at their boundaries, potentially affecting atmospheric composition. The study of these systems can be enhanced by considering their common components and analyzing their differences, which can be visualized on a chart representing the interaction of magnetic and wind pressures.

The Spin-Orbit Proximity Effect has a significant impact on key characteristics of a material that is deposited on another with high spin-orbit coupling. This generated spin-orbit coupling is crucial for achieving novel phases and generating strong magnetic signals in ferromagnetic thin films. As laminated structures consisting of multiple layers of light elements and a ferromagnetic metal have been found to exhibit enhanced spin-orbit coupling, they have been the focus of recent research. Although existing studies have established the presence of spin-orbit coupling in complexes made of heavy metals and a ferromagnetic metal, very little is known regarding combinations of light elemental bi-layers and a ferromagnetic metal. Utilating epitaxial all-sputter technology, we created nickel-cobalt multilayered films capped with various light-element monolayers, and measured their spin-orbit coupling using angular-resolved photoemetry. We observed spin-orbit coupling splitting in cobalt, but not nickel, and the degree of this splitting varied according to the material at the top, demonstrating that these light-element bi-layers can generate spin-orbit coupling.

This study investigates the fractional Schrödinger equation for a generalized Mie-type potential in multiple dimensions, utilizing the Jumarie type fractional derivative. By applying a direct algebraic method, researchers aim to obtain analytic solutions and corresponding fractional energies for the fractional Schrödinger equation. Additionally, both 2D and 3D plots are generated to visualize the behavior of wave functions for a particular potential.

We analyze the effectiveness of penalizing neural network functions to ensure they adhere to a certain degree of smoothness. We establish a crucial link between this continuity and concentration measures, specifically showing that such regularization directly impacts the size of a neural network's response set. We further propose an optimized strategy for determining the force of this penalty and provide evidence of its benefits through numerical experiments.

Recent studies have highlighted the challenge Basque从句 present for state-of-the-art models in Basque NLP, suggesting that Basque presents an uncommon structure known as concord, where the syntactic category of a matrix verb can be determined by that of a subordinate verb embedded within a complement clause. Although the verb in the embedded clause often has its morphological arguments fused together, making it difficult to discern the verb's category from the form of the verb itself, this study investigates whether a Long Short-Term Memory network can successfully predict the syntactic category of a Basque verb, taking into account the category of an embedded verb. This study utilizes a dataset composed of sentence-pairs from the Basque Treebank, where one sentence in each pair differs from the other by the syntactic category of its matrix verb, preparing a subset filtered for sentences containing an embedded clause. The model's ability to accurately distinguish between sentence-pairs is assessed, along with analyses of the subset's characteristics, the influence of corpus size, and the application of pre-trained word embeddings. The results indicate that the LSTM model achieves an accuracy of 70% on the test subset, exceeding chance level at 50%, demonstrating the model's ability to capture some aspects of the phenomenon of concord in Basque.

Astronomical observers are eager to watch HD 80606 b's highly eccentric 43-day orbit that causes significant variations in the planet's apparent brightness. This planet undergoes massive heating as it crosses its host star's path, rising from a nearly complete dark state to a hot state. Precise observations of HD 80606 b's orbit require a high-resolution spectroscopic line analysis, which can provide two vital pieces of information. Firstly, these observations can provide a high-accuracy record of the planet's position in space. Secondly, they can optimize the use of the James Webb Space Telescope, which is scheduled to visit HD 80606 b. This study utilized a high-resolution spectroscopic dataset from VLT/SPHERE that passed by HD 80606. Through the analysis of this data, the researchers found that the observed variations in the planet's brightness consist of multiple overlapping signals. This includes the orbital period of HD 80606 b as well as two additional signals with periods of approximately 12 days. To optimize the use of the telescope, the team found the optimal window for conducting high-energy thermal visits. This involves targeting the planet during specific times of its orbit, which will maximize the amount of information that can be obtained.

This study explores how data-driven models can analyze sport and dance movements to support rehabilitation, and further, how these models can be employed to create customized virtual reality applications for this purpose.

We begin by describing a method to create mixed-dimensional probabilistic models of movement using start and end point data, and show how these models can be used to assess and evaluate motor functionality.

Next, we examine two approaches to representing movements in configuration spaces: sparse linear models and hierarchical generative models, and show how they can be utilized to capture the complexities of movements in dance and sports.

Finally, we explore the potential applications of these models in configuring interactive virtual reality environments for user-generated content to support motor rehabilitation.

Our research offers a variational understanding of the Gamma-convergence for the Γ-convergence of the energy model proposed by Archambault, Juarez, Thomas, and Sifre to model the dynamics of pieces of rigid material, or visco-rigid maps. We demonstrate that this convergence is equivalent to a specific form of convergence, denoted as $\mathcal{H}^1$-convergence, within a class of phase-field approximations of the brittle fracture model introduced by Francfort and Marigo. Similarly, we establish that the convergence of the visco-rigid energy corresponds to a more complex convergence type, which we also define and analyze.

We examine a new type of leptoquark called $\mathcal{L}$ with specific quantum numbers that could be produced during Drell-Yan processes at the Large Hadron Collider. To achieve this, we consider a scenario where $\mathcal{L}$ is capable of decaying into certain quark combinations, and we analyze the processes occurring at the LHC by including initial radiation in Drell-Yan processes. Furthermore, we find that the rate of $q\bar{q}$ annihilation into pairs of $\mathcal{L}$ is highly dependent on the quantum value associated with the leptoquark's charge, and we observe that the Drell-Yan production process significantly contributes to the total cross-section of $\mathcal{L}$ production, and we discuss the results for various possible values of the leptoquark's charge.

Radiation exposure during positron emission tomography (PET) scans restricts their usage for sensitive groups, such as pregnant women and young individuals requiring frequent imaging, due to compromised image quality from lower doses or reduced noise robustness in PET images. To overcome this limitation, we utilized transfer learning to train a neural network on high-quality PET-MR datasets and evaluated its ability to process low-noise, low-dose PET images outside of the training distribution. We developed a new probabilistic neural network that outputs mean and covariance estimates, along with uncertainty maps highlighting unreliable low-dose PET scans. To address the issue of large covariance matrices, we employed low-rank side networks and introduced a new flexible loss function that separately manages deterministic and stochastic losses. Our approach achieved significant performance improvements over external methods on eight completely independent datasets, thus demonstrating the robustness of transfer learning and our proposed model in handling low-dose PET images.

The personalized recommendation system is set to undergo a significant
transformation, with users actively participating in the customization of
recommended content. However, effective customization requires access to
private user data, which must remain secure and under user control. This
project proposes the development of recommendation systems based on user
privacy principles, incorporating features of ownership, confidentiality, and
integrity, along with user involvement in the customization process. Furthermore, we outline key research areas needed to bring this conceptual framework
to reality.

This paper investigates the concept of centering theory, a prominent framework that explains how language users track conversational focus, in relation to contemporary machine learning-based coreference resolution models. We, as linguists, are studying the connections between the principles of centering and the mechanisms employed by state-of-the-art coreference resolution systems. While the principle of minimizing discourse cost, central to the centering theory, has a direct counterpart in coreference resolution systems through the propagation of classification results, other aspects require further analysis. We propose several hypotheses to clarify the relationship between the systems' mechanisms and the centering principles, and to validate these, we present an experimental approach that involves modifying system outputs in line with centering's predictability and focus shift rules. Ultimately, our research aims to provide a foundational understanding of context in coreference resolution systems and inform the development of more context-aware methods.

We investigate how certain parameters influence the complexity of solving upward planarity, a variation of directed graph drawing problems. Upward planarity determines if edges can be routed using monotone paths that maintain planarity. We establish that certain parameters, such as those related to vertex and edge properties, allow for fixed-parameter tractability in solving the problem. We also provide an algorithm for spiral upward planarity based on certain parameter values. Moreover, we demonstrate that parameterized inapproximability arises from the values of certain parameters, and we explore how these findings can be applied to other graph drawing problems.

This setup report outlines our approach to automatically configuring a target architecture for upcoming research. Particularly challenging aspects of this project, such as developing a custom FPGA bitstream, are detailed. We specifically focus on implementing a custom interconnect called RaIDSL, for which we outline an entire flow from design to configuration.

This study examines how Lie algebra operators evolve over time within an $N$-body system that utilizes simple commutation rules, specifically in an $A_N$ truncation. 
We investigate an initial state, defined by a single product of k近 neighbor interactions, and observe its rapid expansion into more complex, longer-length operators. 
Our work provides analytical proof that in a quantum chaotic system, near neighbor interactions rapidly give way to globally connected operators. 
We also explore an alternative scenario where operator length growth is limited, leading to the development of bound states. 
This research has significant implications for quantum simulation experiments and theoretical aspects such as KKO duality and the chaotic behavior of Einstein's field equations.

Recently, WiFi sensing has gained significant interest due to its ability to detect presence, classify individuals and estimate distances. This report presents initial findings in exploring the WiFi-based distance estimation between a device and a mobile node through direction of arrival (DOA) mapping. We collected a unique dataset consisting of 256 spatial points, each recorded from a different angle, to analyze if supervised machine learning models, specifically linear regression and support vector regression, could accurately predict distances using this data. Our results show that while these algorithms performed better than random guessing, they were not as effective in doing so.

Assessing supermassive black holes in the galactic center has been hindered by the intense emissions from surrounding jets and a dense ring, known as the Dyson Shell, formed when stars orbiting the nucleus are consumed. We explore a Dyson Shell formed around a stellar mass black hole at the galaxy's core through hydrodynamic simulations of ionized gas. The simulations consider the emissions from accretion onto the black hole, as well as from photoevaporation driven by the black hole's ultraviolet radiation. Depending on whether the Shell maintains its shape, it either stabilizes as a spherical blob or breaks apart due to the force of the black hole's radiation. Furthermore, we analyze how the Shell reacts to a jet emitted from the black hole, exhibiting two distinct end states: one with a compressed, dense region at the pole, and another with a dense equatorial region, effectively acting as a natural shield against the jet. These features could potentially be observed by the next generation of radio telescopes, such as the next generation very large array, and have implications for interpreting observations of galaxies with active nuclei.

Network operators are responsible for delivering network services that meet agreed-upon criteria, known as detecting Service Level Agreement (SLA) breaches. To achieve this, they employ various monitoring techniques, including active and passive methods. This paper proposes a novel approach to SLA breach detection, leveraging peer-to-peer (P2P) technology. By combining the capabilities of passive monitoring with the flexibility of active probing, a unique active-passive detection system is designed. To evaluate its effectiveness, an implementation is created and tested on an emulated network, combining results from multiple uncorrelated links. This method yields an overall breach detection system that is at least as accurate as purely active probing, while significantly reducing the associated costs.

The exceptional performance of energy recovery linacs depends heavily on high beam current design choices. Unfortunately, conventional linear design tends to exacerbate beam breakup instability due to its flat energy distribution. Studies indicate that modifying ERL beam profiles could effectively mitigate this issue, although the optimal profile for reducing BBU remains unexplored. This study analyses impact of various design principles on beam breakup instability, finding that non-linear and spiral layout designs provide significant advantages over traditional linear arrangements. Enhanced mixing and natural damping effects in non-linear and spiral designs offer improved stability, whereas increased path length in a spiral design contributes additional beam breakup instability damping. As a result, BBU limits in non-linear and spiral designs are found to be 1-2 orders of magnitude greater than their linear counterparts, making these designs promising new options for high-performance ERLs.

To improve the understanding of 3D track reconstruction in particle detectors, a study was conducted on identifying neutral particles that don't leave any visible traces. Since these particles can't be visually tracked, they need to be indirectly tracked by interacting with a detector and producing visible debris. Because measuring these interactions takes time and reduces the performance of the device, it's crucial to find materials with high trackability and low interaction cross-sections. As many materials have been already studied, there's a significant focus on finding suitable materials that aren't yet fully explored. In this study, we measured the neutron interaction cross-section by using 3D reconstructed tracks and analyzing events with those tracks. Our results, which showed total cross-section value of 0.41 barn for protons on the scintillator, were based on 3D reconstructed tracks and a specific cut on those tracks, and had a statistical uncertainty of 0.02 barn.

To understand the process of planetary formation, it is crucial to comprehend how sub-micro meter sized dust particles bond together to form larger bodies. The sticking properties of these tiny particles are heavily influenced in the warm environments found in the inner regions of protoplanetary discs, where high temperatures can cause them to melt or vaporize, undermining their cohesion. In a laboratory experiment, researchers investigated how fine grains of forsterite, enstatite, and silicate affect particle cohesion as temperatures rise up to 900 K, mimicking the conditions found in some protoplanetary discs. They measured particle cohesion by observing how far surface layers could be indented without breaking through to a freshly exposed surface. The results revealed that while particle cohesion generally decreases with rising temperatures, there can be unexpected changes, likely due to alterations in the particles' crystalline structure. Notably, all three materials lost their sticking properties before reaching 600 K, which represents a critical temperature threshold for planetary formation processes. This finding has significant implications for theories of planetary formation, suggesting that certain mechanisms, such as the accumulation of particles due to settling and phase transitions, may need to be reevaluated.

The local Fisher distinction analysis method is a well-established visualization and dimension reduction technique, with numerous implementations in Python but limited options in the R language. This paper introduces an R package for conducting local Fisher distinction analysis, featuring a function that utilizes the 'optlink' library to minimize the objective function and generates scatter plot visualizations with the 'ggallinea' package.

Imitation learning has emerged as a key method for enabling robots to learn tasks efficiently from human demonstrations, leveraging their ability to capture complex skills and physical constraints embedded in demonstrated trajectories. However, simply copying these trajectories can be hampered by environmental obstacles and may result in suboptimal solutions due to the nonlinear nature of constraint enforcement. To address these issues, we extend the Ewald-Knot method for constraint enforcement, allowing for selective modeling of nonlinear constraints and local obstacle avoidance. This approach allows for the demonstration of feasible trajectories in obstacle-free environments, where the robot learns to avoid obstacles en route to the target. The enhanced method is also capable of enforcing a broader range of constraints, including task-related ones, to produce efficient and feasible solutions. The method's effectiveness is demonstrated through imitating complex tasks, such as swinging a pendulum and following curved paths, even in the presence of obstacles.

To advance the computational efficiency of QCD processes at the LHC, particularly for beyond-standard-model searches, precise predictions are crucial. A key area of research involves massless particle interactions, central to many complex processes. This study provides the required data by calculating the analytic form of a specific one-loop object, a two-gluon-emission vertex, in N=4 supersymmetric Yang-Mills theory. Offering a parameterized result, our calculation contributes to fundamental constants and is presented in a form that, when combined with known two-point functions, can aid in determining other one-loop objects, thereby facilitating highly accurate predictions for massless particle interactions.

Within this research, we've established that the Rashba Hubbard model at the topological phase exhibits superfluid characteristics in both the repulsive and attractive interaction regimes. Specifically, we've demonstrated that the spin-singlet t-superfluid state persists within the attractive interaction regime despite the presence of level crossing. Furthermore, we've identified that Rashba Rashba superfluids exhibit topological properties, whereas those resulting from lattice Rashba rotations are non-trivial. Topological Rashba Rashba superfluidity can be achieved directly from experimental samples by gradually altering lattice parameters and rotating the system.

By combining terahertz spectroscopy and scanning tunneling microscopy, we reexamined data from a cuprate superconductor, revealing a previously unnoticed feature. This feature, which appears just outside the superconducting energy gap and displays six-fold rotational symmetry, cannot be accounted for by the intrinsic superconducting gap. Our hypothesis posits that this anomaly is, in fact, evidence for a vortex state that competes with the superconducting gap. As we vary the material's doping level, we observe a shift in the vortex state from a square grid pattern to this more intrinsic, six-fold symmetric state.

We investigate the effects of molten polymer brushes on the movement of spherical objects moving at slow speeds. A key feature of these brushes is that they are composed of highly stretched polymers. We find that regardless of the shape or size of the underlying surface, there is a spherical region around any point on that surface where the movement of a sphere is restricted. We derive a precise mathematical formula that outlines the boundary of this region, taking into consideration the material properties of the polymer and the size of the sphere.

A graph G is considered trim if it has at least three vertices and no isolated points or edges. This project focuses on identifying all trim finite graphs with a specific property: a trimmed set K is essential in determining any vertex by a unique shortest path to each member of K, with at least two vertices following this rule. Projects aiming to identify trimmed finite graphs will contribute to the broader understanding of trimmed graphs, a newly explored topic in current research.

Researchers utilized the Fermi-LAT gamma-ray data to develop a machine learning model based on support vector regression, which identified the influence of variable sources on the global all-sky map. A traditional point-source model created a precise baseline image but failed to capture variations. In contrast, an SVR model generated an inaccurate yet variable map, illustrating unexplained residuals as dark red and blue areas. By analyzing the model's parameters, researchers found that 15 regions with significant flux changes over time contributed most to the variable signal, while many other regions showed moderate variability. Furthermore, an all-sky map constructed from the variable source model demonstrated a similar cosmic ray belt but with a reduced intensity.

Set partial ordering concepts are commonly employed to model diverse scenarios in several fields, such as they appear in multiple applications. 
Given a set, a monarchy is defined as a specific type of partial ordering that excludes certain relationships, and our research concentrates on direct methods to solve optimization problems over set-valued functions. 
We develop an algorithm to solve a broad class of optimization problems, and establish that under specific conditions, its solution equates to the original problem's solution. 
This solution involves solving multiple smoother optimization problems with a smoother objective and gradient, and we provide theoretical and numerical evidence of its benefits, particularly its ability to handle non-differentiable functions like the maximum function and efficient computation through parallelization. 
Our approach is empirically shown to outperform existing techniques and effectively solve challenging problems. 
These results are Shavitt, D., Kerenis, G., & Shwartz, Z. (2019) - Optimizing over Set Monarchies in Partial Orderings.

We introduce a novel term, binary aster, to describe uncataloged and unmarked double stars on modern, high-resolution survey images, which currently hinder the efficiency of astrometric analyses. These small features pose significant obstacles to precise measurements. We suggest an automated method to detect binary asters in vast datasets, and illustrate our approach with pan-STARRS1 data. By combining existing catalogues with relative astrometry, we were able to systematically remove over 11 million binary aster in 130 nights of data, significantly enhancing the efficiency of our subsequent analyses. However, the elimination of these artifacts required developing accurate and robust catalogues, which on average improved our magnitudes by 0.047 and color measurements by 0.006. Notably, the reduction in scatter for bright stars reached as much as 0.003 in both cases. Although the increase in computational time was marginal, rising to 0.013 minutes in some instances, we observed a substantial reduction in computational scatter from 0.00019 to 0.00017.

This research paper offers novel statistical methods for analyzing data from networks where the outcome of interest is connected to the observed variables of agents within those networks. The study's findings go beyond prior work by making no assumptions about the structure of the network, enabling estimates and statistical inferences for both linear and non-linear components of a regression model. The model's flexibility permits the separation of linear and non-linear aspects, with implications for understanding peer influences in high school smoking behaviors. The estimation procedure is consistent, scalable, with performance validated through numerical experiments. The study's methodology can be effectively implemented, as shown in the analysis of peer influences in high school smoking behaviors. The study's findings cannot be attributed solely to bias, with evidence supporting the presence of non-linear effects. The study's data is abundant, with the sample size exceeding the number of parameters to be estimated. The performance of the estimator is assessed through simulations, with results demonstrating low bias and reasonable variability.

The concept of Spatially Varied Signals has significant potential in areas such as cognitive radio and radio astronomy. However, their characterization and processing remain underdeveloped due to the complexity of modeling and the difficulty of obtaining a closed-form solution for real-time applications. This paper focuses on developing a variance profile model to represent SVS and provides new mathematical proofs for random noise. Specifically, we have developed detailed expressions for the covariance profile and standard deviation profile. To detect a weak signal embedded in noise, we have analyzed and derived risk functions for two signal processing methods, including a minimum variance method. Our research enables a practical application of SVS processing, particularly in signal detection using the variance profile approach.

We've created an open-source suite of Python scripts and a user-friendly web interface that streamlines the creation, manipulation, and visualization of two-dimensional spectral arrays. This system is specifically designed to simplify the exploration and visualization of spectroscopic observations made by astronomical telescopes, yet it has broader applications in fields such as biology and chemistry. Furthermore, we've contributed to the astropy-package and developed nextrepresent.org as examples of our representation tools.

The Southern Atlantic Ocean began to form due to a North-South stretching force that weakened the Peri-Gondwanan continental margin, specifically in the South Brazil Uplift area. This weakening was balanced by compressive forces acting on the São Francisco Craton from the northwest. Pre-rift sediments from the Cenozoic era in the South Brazil Uplift show the effects of extensional regimes that were influenced by R1 and R3 quadrants, likely caused by a stress rotation axis in the East. This stress acted perpendicular to the South Brazil Uplift's main trend and was responsible for normal and strike-slip faults and N-S well profiles. These normal faults created local N-S and NE-SW pull-apart basins. The stress pattern in the South Brazil Uplift can be attributed to the shear along the Brazil Uplift-Gondwanan margin, which should have generated N-S normal faults and the observed quadrantal stress distribution, resulting from the South America-Africa separation.

Information maximization is a well-established, versatile learning technique that has been applied successfully to computer vision tasks, including segmenting images. It is also capable of handling complex patterns, such as those found at the boundaries in medical images. This work demonstrates that a simple Information Maximization pre-training step can enhance the performance of downstream segmentaion tasks when using lightweight convolutional neural networks. Researchers have further explored how learned features relate to information theory by examining what kind of information is captured. This investigation has led to the development of an information-assisted feature importance method and shows that incorporating the principles of information maximization can lead to more meaningful boundary-aware features. To explicitly optimize these features at the boundaries without compromising the overall efficiency, researchers have created an additional module based on information theory and integrated it into an downstream segmentaion framework. The results indicate that this proposed framework delivers state-of-the-art performance on multiple datasets, including ATLAS, PanoSeg, and Panaderia.

Building a conversational agent that can effectively engage in a role-playing game, particularly one as complex as Dungeons and Dragons, poses significant challenges.
Successfully achieving this would require the agent to:
1.
Share the fantasy world's knowledge base, including characters, creatures, and physical laws.
2.
Draw from this knowledge to create realistic interactions.
3.
Make informed decisions guided by the game's narrative.
We investigated each of these challenges separately, focusing on separate components.
To address the first challenge, we collected and annotated a customized dataset containing essential information about the fantasy world.
To successively address challenges two and three, we explored methods to train the agent using Intents learned through natural language processing.
These Intents serve as both communicative tools and guiding mechanisms.
For further control, we introduced a theory-of-mind model, allowing the agent to learn non-linearly and make adjustments based on the Intents.
We assessed the agent's performance in experimenting with different theory-of-mind models.
To collect data, we conducted sessions with real players of an online version of the game, incorporating our agent.
We analyzed the resulting dialogue and scored Intents based on their clarity, relevance, and utility.
We established a baseline using maximum-entropy classification and generated answers through rule-based methods.
To improve answers, we employed neural network models, while our theory-of-mind model was assessed based on accurate predictions made during the game.

Despite significant progress in lexicon construction, a remaining challenge persists in identifying lexicons that reflect semantic shifts. Many methodologies produce a lexicon, but only a few explicitly generate lexicons tailored to a particular meaning. This paper introduces a method for detecting lexical semantic variation, which encompasses the evolution of words' meanings over time. This method first divides corpus history into distinct periods and then creates a lexicon. To test its effectiveness, the team artificially induced lexical and semantic variations in two corpora spanning 12 years, and compared the resulting lexicons to a baseline constructed from the entire corpus. The results showed that their method could distinguish between different types of variation and was particularly proficient in capturing terms related to varying concepts.

We suggest a new way to describe particle movement, which is missing from the standard particle density function. Our proposal, which includes directional particle movement, is then compared to the widely used quasi-particle distribution function.

The three-dimensional structure and complexity of knotted proteins stand in contrast to the flat, two-dimensional arrangement of their genetic code. Researchers believe that the formation of these unusual three-dimensional shapes occurs as the protein transitions from its synthesized state. Identifying the specific folded shapes and knot patterns during this formation process remains a significant challenge due to difficulties in modeling the entangled movement of polymer chains. A novel mathematical approach, combining simplicity with reliability, is presented for analyzing the folding formation processes of polymer chains. This method is then applied to study the knot formation patterns in certain trivalent-tripartite structures and determines the most efficient folding pathways for multiple structures, resulting in distinct shape formations. Notably, one structure follows a specific formation sequence, resulting in a particular knot pattern, while another structure exhibits a more complex folding process and distinct knot formation stages.

To address the anomaly in the cosmic tension, we introduce a new dark energy model that appears early in the universe's history. We then examine how this model affects the Planck and Baryon Oscillation Spectroscopic Cooperation (BOSS) data, particularly in relation to the Hubble constant. By comparing our early dark energy model to $\Lambda$CDM, we determine that if the early dark energy density fraction is between $10^{-3}$ and $0.1$, it can reduce the $\sigma_8$ tension to its observed levels, though this comes with a restriction on the universe's current expansion rate, $H_0$, of 67.4$^{+1.4}_{-1.3}$ km/s/Mpc, from our model's analysis.

Building on previous work, this paper extends the definition of symplectic mapping category groups to include deformation-equivalence, then applies these groups to analyze the symplectic geometry of blowups of tori and rational surfaces, as well as compares these geometries through their symplectic mapping category groups.

A rigorous mathematical analysis has been performed to enhance the understanding of the Nambu-Goldstone theorem, which establishes a link between symmetry breaking and the appearance of massless particles in quantum field theory. Although there's an existing proof of this theorem in a mathematical context, our investigation delves into the underlying mechanisms and provides multiple, in-depth descriptions of the relevant Hilbert space subspaces associated with symmetry breaking. Furthermore, our analysis includes the derivation of both a modified, more intricate form of the theorem applicable to both relativistic and nonrelativistic theories, as well as a simplified, abstract version with overarching implications of the proof. A significantly streamlined, user-friendly proof has been presented to clarify the original, more involved argument.

Recent advances in creating hypothetical datasets have been shown to be effective in enhancing model performance, but the process of crafting numerous hypothetical examples has been time-consuming and cumbersome. To address this issue, we introduce a new framework called DISCO, which is a method that generates and distills a set of hypothetical phrases in an automatic and efficient manner. When applied to the task of low-resource machine translation, this innovative approach results in significant improvements in performance, with our method surpassing traditional techniques and achieving remarkable gains of up to 1.4 on average and 2.8 in specific scenarios.

In this study, we offer proofs for the total colorability of specific types of circulant graphs, including double path expansions of cycles, multi-edged cycles, and 4-tuples of cycles. Additionally, we determine the exact total chromatic indices for these graphs under conditions of equitability in coloring.

Research into remote epitaxy is being significantly influenced by recent breakthrough们在 ultrathin films on graphene. Researchers have developed precise measurement techniques and high-speed atomic microscopy images that allow them to determine the strain in these thin layers. However, until now, there was little understanding of how remote epitaxy interacts with other modes of epitaxy when growing thicker films. Through a theoretical model incorporating finite element method, we link the equilibrium between remote epitaxy and other modes of epitaxy to a key material property and the thickness of films being deposited. Specifically, we found that while remote epitaxy prevails in thin films, others begin to dominate as the films thicken. By experiment and calculation, we discovered that certain Heusler films on graphene/Al$_2$O$_3$ substrates can be engineered to exist in different states depending on their thickness. Control of this equilibrium is achieved by changing the crystallographic orientation of the Heusler films. Ultimately, this has significant implications for using graphene as a template in growing complex multilayer structures with remote epitaxy.

A code is referred to as $ \mathbb{Z}_p $ $ \mathbb{Z}_{p^2} $-linear if its generator matrix comprises two parts, where the first part has a prime base $ p $ and the second part can be ignored when $ p $ is greater than $ s $. The dimension and kernel of $ \mathbb{Z}_p $ $ \mathbb{Z}_{p^2} $-linear codes are defined and analyzed, and a formula is established to calculate their size.

A novel approach, polymer plugs technology, is transforming the recovery process in oil wells by injecting biodegradable material串 into existing reservoirs. The key to the success of this method lies in determining the ideal polymer profile for blockage formation, which not only boosts displacement efficiency but also minimizes the risk of well failures. This study leverates the principles of polymer flow and the fading properties of the reservoir to model the complex interaction between oil and the polymer block, subsequently using numerical methods to solve the formed equations. The resulting analysis yields a set of optimal conditions, taking into consideration various operational factors, and is illustrated with a specific scenario before being applied to a real-world well in the Dohain field in Algeria.

A single label often fails to adequately describe an image containing objects of multiple categories, which hinders the use of such images for multi-label tasks. This paper aims to provide a method for extracting multi-label samples from images labeled with a single label. The proposed approach, called Multi-Label Extraction (MLE), leverages image embeddings and attention mechanisms to identify and include region proposals corresponding to other potential objects within the label's category. An alternative version of MLE is also explored, utilizing a ranking loss to produce an image embedding representing all detected objects. Experimental results on PASCAL VOC 2012 and COCO 2014 datasets demonstrate that MLE can effectively generate multi-label samples from images with a single label. Furthermore, MLE is shown to be a reliable method for augmenting multi-label datasets, yielding improvements in performance when tested on PASCAL VOC 2012.

This research provides an upper energy bound for the time-fractional Allen-Cahn, Caginalp, and Heun-Cahn equations, utilizing the Riemann-Liouville derivative. The upper energy bound is related to the Caputo derivative of the time fraction $\alpha$ and satisfies a zero upper energy bound at the time origin for all time. The study also demonstrates that the derived upper energy bound cannot be replaced with the classical whole number order time derivative of the solution. Nor can it be related to an lower energy bound for 0 < \alpha < 1. Furthermore, the paper proves that the equality of the derived upper energy bound can be achieved by an exact solution to the time-fractional Heun-Cahn equation, and obtains a fundamental inequality connecting the upper energy bound with certain norms of the Riemann-Liouville fractional integral, and the solution's fractional Caputo derivative. The research may lay the foundation for a significant research direction in the field of HPC modeling, simulation, and visualization of phase-field models. The related findings are not applicable to the time-fractional Heun-Cahn Glancing equation. The research also introduces the concept of energy barrier in the context of HPC simulation and visualization.

The GNS construction connects abstract states to concrete observables within a C*-algebra, a process fundamental to quantum mechanics. We look into this procedure through the lens of higher category theory, specifically using 2-categorical structures, and aim to clarify the underlying mathematical principles through this theoretical framework.

In nearby radio galaxies and active nuclei, the energy sources are highly abundant and observable in visible light, energy spectra, and radio energy. Our analysis of the X-ray and radio data focuses on identifying patterns of excess energy in these regions, particularly in the energy range between ultraviolet to X-rays, often attributed to charged particles with high energy in quasi-disks suspended by magnetic fields along the edges. These "fuzzies" are proposed as the primary origin of excess energy in galaxy nuclei. During a detailed examination of nearby active nuclei in spiral galaxies with significant "fuzzies", we found a strong correlation between the intensity of gamma-rays and the high-energy cutoff in electron distributions, suggesting that gamma-rays are likely produced at the boundaries of these structures through interactions of high-energy protons or electrons with surrounding gas clouds. The expected energy levels of gamma-rays in this model are below detection limits for many systems but may explain the unusually low energy levels observed in M104 and similar galaxies. Furthermore, we anticipate that future observations with more sensitive detectors will provide better evidence for this hypothesis.

This research refines key concepts from Admati (1985) and Fama (1989) by formulating a profit-maximizing portfolio problem, taking into account final wealth as the objective, the efficient frontier, and risk aversion. We leverage stochastic optimization to create a comprehensive model that incorporates these elements and risk avoidance, using its solutions to explore various portfolio allocation strategies. We apply this approach to develop a new method for creating performance-predictive portfolios and a more efficient way to construct benchmark portfolios. To validate our method, we use mean-variance optimization, a power utility approach, and real-world market data. Our results show that our stochastic framework outperforms traditional methods in both studies. Additionally, our new algorithm for constructing benchmark portfolios achieves comparable performance to established methods but at a significantly lower computational cost.

Mitigating noise interference via deep learning can lead to the model memorizing noise patterns, known as noise tampering, which necessitates addressing with methods capable of mitigating such interference learning within deep neural networks. This research utilizes heart sound signals as a test case to analyze the coexistence of noise and musical patterns, employing multiple signal processing techniques to remove redundant information and facilitating the clearance of the signal, thereby enabling a simpler neural network to effectively extract pertinent features and minimize reliance on high-frequency components. Consequently, this approach enables a neural network to clearaneously learn amidst noisy signals without becoming clouded by high-frequency noise.

The proliferation of mobile technology and smart devices has drastically changed how people interact, making them essential for everyday activities. Wearable devices have gained significant importance as they monitor, track health metrics and provide alerts based on collected information. Although these technologies rely on extensive user data for safety, privacy concerns arise from potential hacking risks. Federated learning offers a novel approach, enabling efficient, secure training of machine learning models on distributed devices without sharing information. This section introduces FedHealth, a federated transfer learning framework that leverages smart device technology to enhance healthcare models while ensuring user privacy.

This study classifies portfolio optimization strategies with higher order moments including skewness and kurtosis to aid Hedge Fund practitioners in navigating various paradigms and methodologies. Key research approaches, such as utility theory and multi-objective optimization, are reviewed, with an examination of their benefits and limitations.

In string compactifications, we suggest that dark energy marks the universe's end, 
potentially triggered by decompactification, addressing the cosmological coincidence problem. 
We SUGRA analysis reveals that dark energy arises when extra dimensions grow, 
leading to a universe with the size of Planck units. Our findings indicate that anti-de Sitter spaces are unlikely, 
but in conformal field theory, dark energy results from a shift in scale invariance.

This document explains our newly developed tool, SAT - a completely automated system for researching and analyzing financial data. SAT offers a straightforward method for studying complex market phenomena, reducing errors caused by manual data interpretation. Once built, SAT can be deployed on various computers, from personal laptops to server arrays, for real-time analysis.

The optimal switching control problem on a fixed time interval is examined.  
Various conditions are established for several types of control costs, which vary  
significantly with the direction of switching. Several convergence results are  
proved for a series of control problems with fluidized costs and have a dual  
purpose: they offer some unidentified value functions and optimal strategies for  
the aforementioned cases. Several further results are also established.

This paper explores the possibility of scalar leptoquarks interacting with neutrinos and quarks, potentially being discovered through the method of pair creation. We are studying untagged processes where the final products consist of four jets and minimal missing energy. A significant challenge in analyzing these processes is distinguishing signal from background, especially since the underlying physics involves indistinguishable leptoquarks decaying hadronically. A method has been developed involving missing transverse momentum and specific jet configurations to reduce the dominant top-quark and W-boson backgrounds. However, these techniques also suppress the leptoquark signal. A theoretical calculation of the scalar LQ cross-section and mass relationship has been formulated, utilizing both parton and hadron-level cuts. A method for estimating the statistical significance of a discovery using the topological hypothesis testing approach has been introduced, considering the dominant backgrounds. A map indicating the minimum significant CL value achievable for each possible LQ mass through untagged process analysis has been created, showing a minimum of 3 significant CL at 2.57 times the LQ mass for significant discovery. Furthermore, a method involving machine learning techniques has been proposed to enhance the analysis, potentially reaching 3 significant CL at 2.33 times the LQ mass.

Due to rapid advancements, modern analytical instruments can collect life science samples and perform chromatography on them at a speed of several hundred times per second, and each collection and measurement generates a very high-dimensional time-series data that is typical for co-varying features in a dynamic subspace. To effectively model and analyze this data, we need algorithms capable of reducing dimensionality, segmenting time periods, and interpreting the data within its specific context. To address this challenge, we have developed an asynchronous guided learning framework which employs an autoencoder architecture and utilizes expert feedback to reduce dimensionality, segment time periods, and interpret the data simultaneously.
