Deep learning-based medical image segmentation techniques achieve remarkable performance, but they depend on large datasets for precise training. Unfortunately, manual annotation is extremely time-consuming, making little progress toward several tasks feasible. To address this, consistency regularization has been developed as a means of expanding limited labeled datasets. This approach was first introduced and subsequently refined with the purpose of introducing technical terminology related to medical image analysis.

The ATLAS Jet Trigger System at the LHC needs a significant upgrade to handle increased data processing demands. To meet this challenge, a new prototype called ATLAS-Ultrascale has been developed, utilizing Intel's Ultrascale FPGA. This prototype features an advanced FPGA with 6.5 million logic elements and 4.4GB of on-board memory, enabling it to handle complex data processing tasks. This prototype also adopts an open-source design, software, and driver framework, allowing for easy expansion and integration of new features. This design significantly reduces the time and resources required for future system upgrades. This prototype represents a major step forward in the development of the ATLAS Jet Trigger System and paves the way for a significant performance boost using state-of-the-art technology.

This paper describes the Articulated Neural Visualization (ANR) network, a novel method for generating avatars through neural rendering. Unlike previous methods that treat characters as a single rigid entity, ANR incorporates a full body optimization of an articulated human model, making it possible to create realistic virtual avatars from monocular videos. An key innovation of our approach is the use of ANR features to simultaneously achieve a high-fidelity rendering and accurate alignment of the NeRF model with the video frames, which eliminates the need for the 125-K Euler Anger input used in the ANIME-NERF framework. We outperform the ANIME-NERF baseline in our internal evaluations and make our code available at https://github.com/hjdwz/ANR.

A critical aspect of understanding complex systems, whether they are highly chaotic or simply non-linear, is differentiating between disordered and patterned relationships between the system's components. To address this, we have created an innovative and interpretable algorithm based on graph-based representation, which can accurately measure how the system interacts and has been effective when applied to an atomic system exhibiting highly chaotic or quasicrystalline behavior. Our results have also provided a chalcogen transition point that divides these two dynamic behaviors, and we have observed that the characteristics identified by this algorithm can reveal the intricate relationships between the system's components in ways that other methods struggle to do.

Consider a scenario where independent and identically distributed random variables $X_1, \dots, X_n$ come from a distribution $X$, which is either a direct draw from a non-mixture distribution $Y$ or the average of $k$ independent draws from distribution $Y$, based on a probabilistic factor $\lambda$. Given known values of $k$ and $\lambda$, this paper develops an estimator for $\theta = E\left(\mu(E(X_i) | \Lambda = \lambda)\right)$ using maximum likelihood estimation, utilizing observed values $x_1, \dots, x_n$. The proposed estimator is supported by a Bayesian alternative, a consistency proof, and an asymptotic normality demonstration, accompanied by simulation studies.

Knowledge tracing is an educational data mining technique used to track a student's knowledge development. It is essential for adapting learning to individual students' needs and is typically applied in adaptive learning systems. In this research, we present and evaluate several knowledge tracing models based on neural networks, including a simple model and more complex variants. For exact replication of our methods, we have developed and made available the PyKT library and associated scripts on Maven, which utilize concepts from attention mechanisms and long short-term memory networks.

Given a variety $X$ over $\mathbb{C}$, we demonstrate that a key property previously established by Kauffman and Ogus implies elliptic operators are those which are closed. Consequently, on a non-compact algebraic variety, all elliptic operators are closed.

Microsoft's TheoreProver Assistant (TaProothe) has been designed to serve as a versatile standard for exchanging arguments validated by SMT solvers, with a specific focus on semantic clarity and generality across different proof formats. Alethe, a TaProothe implementation, not only functions as a distinct solver but also acts as a format that can convert complex arguments from other tools, such as CVC3, E, and Z3, with few exceptions. Alethe is also set to serve as a default validated format for the C11 Challenge.

This research focuses on federated learning, a method that trains machine learning models on local devices and combines them into a single model. We present an improvement to a previously developed buffered asynchronous federated learning technique, which allows for unrestricted gradient changes on client devices. The technique is also made more computationally efficient and one that can be applied to real-world client devices. When testing was conducted against established buffered and non-buffered federated learning methods, our research demonstrated superior results in terms of classification accuracy, classification F1 score, energy consumption, and runtime.

Recently, end-to-end neural automatic speech recognition systems have been widely adopted due to their superior performance, although they face challenges with far-field recordings that require considerable computational resources and a detailed acoustic model. To address this, a two-stage approach has become popular, combining a coarse model for initial far-field recognition and a fine model for final city-center recognition. Furthermore, this study explores a cross-language transfer strategy using a two-stage model. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of this method in low-resource translation scenarios when combined with monolingual fine-tuning. To enhance modeling efficiency, a two-stage system is proposed. It employs a lightweight Convolutive Transducer for the transfer model and a detailed Multi-Efficient Former for the fine model. Formally evaluated results show significant improvements in the proposed method compared to the previous state-of-the-art.

Graph mining applications demand representations that capture a network's geometry and role-based architecture, and embedding techniques are proving effective in this area. To assess embedding methods' performance, we introduce a comprehensive dataset, Twitch Players, comprising a real-world graph with intricate properties. As the first in English of its kind, this dataset enables a standardized evaluation of node embedding techniques. It is notable for containing three distinct communities, diverse node degrees, and role-based classifications, and we assessed seven popular node embedding methods, resulting in our conclusion that the Bilinear Pooling method outperformed the competition in this evaluation.

Our study focuses on the distinction between $f_2(1420)$ and $f_2(1440)$, with some previous research interpreting signals found near the $\eta_c\bar c$ threshold in searches for the $f_2(1420)$ as $f_2(1440)$. We have conducted an in-depth investigation of the $f_2(1420)$'s properties by using data from $B^0\to \pi^+\pi^-\pi^0\overline{K}^*0, B^0\to \overline{K}^*0\overline{K}^*0$ and $B^+\to K^+(1450)K^-$ decays. Moreover, we have gathered available data from literature and conducted analyses to report new findings, specifically on the mass, width, and mass ratio of these resonances.

We propose a new concept, the Dark Dimension, which suggests a primordial dimension invisible to us, yet accessible to a vast number of primordial black holes. We analyze the dark substance, which comprises the majority of these black holes, and discuss the relationship between the Dark Dimension and the Swampland Program's theoretical constraints. We investigate the possibility of dark matter evolving from unique, destroyed swamps in the five-dimensional Swampland, and how this relates to the Dimensional Deconstruction Conjecture. Furthermore, we compare the notions of the Swampland, Dark Dimension, and Substance, and offer the idea that unique destruction of two-swamps in higher dimensions may lead to a concentration of matter in new dimensions, accessible to numerous primordial black holes in our three-dimensional universe.

A novel algorithm for precise force control in SAAs has been developed, utilizing an innovative Elastic Transmission Force Estimator (ETFE) in conjunction with rate feedback. Addressing the challenges of accuracy imposed by data processing delays and nonlinear factors such as friction and actuator saturation, this approach effectively mitigates their impact on the system's performance. By leveraging the properties of ETFE, closed-loop system stability is guaranteed through the application of a semi-global asymptotic stability theory, ensuring optimal performance through careful design of the control law. Numerical simulations and experimental tests on an SAA-based manipulator demonstrate the effectiveness of this method in achieving highly accurate force tracking even under substantial disturbances.

Polystyrene spheres with adjustable magnetic properties are employed to investigate the structure of non-magnetically interacted spheres within a liquid medium, specifically within rafts formed at the liquid's surface. The examination of these groups reveals distinct regions; some contain no pairs of spheres experiencing magnetic attraction, increasing significantly near the raft's boundaries. These three types of regions can be distinguished by their unique height, density, and structural characteristics. Investigating the arrangement of spheres within these distinct regions reveals that each exhibits characteristic features, particularly near the raft's boundaries.

Lattice gauge theory research has a long history of studying SU(Nc) theories with scalar fields, with the focus recently shifting towards understanding their Higgs phases and potential applications to QCD with multiple scalars. This study presents an in-depth lattice investigation of SU(Nc) theories with a degenerate set of scalar masses. By analyzing an order parameter that distinguishes the confining and Higgs phases, we constructed a phase diagram for a range of Nc values. Our results indicate that a first-order phase transition separates the confining and Higgs phases for all Nc values tested. For sufficiently low values of the beta parameter, we found evidence of an intermediate Coulomb phase for all but the smallest value of Nc. This research contributes to the ongoing lattice exploration required to determine the nature of the Minkowski vacuum in models with multiple scalar fields.

When using reinforcement learning to train robots, it is essential to scale up the state and action spaces to accommodate the complexity of real-world applications. In particular, learning Gaussian process models allows us to approximate the transition and reward dynamics of an robot's operation, enabling more efficient policy development. Building on this concept, we have developed an algorithm that combines Gaussian process models with temporal difference learning to train a robot in a sparse data environment. This new approach was successfully applied to guide a marine robot, AUV-HUNT, demonstrating its effectiveness in creating precise policies with limited data.

Recent research has revitalized interest in sorting networks, a theoretical model used to analyze the limitations of parallel algorithms for permutation networks and sorting networks. Modern applications, such as hardware implementations of hash tables, often rely on binary searching networks, and historically, studies on arrangement networks were based on non-rigorous heuristics. This project aims to develop a precise, mathematically sound method for analyzing arrangement network performance within this framework. Building upon De's recent breakthrough, we enhance the best-known binary arrangement network in depth d ≥ 5 from log^-(n) to 2^-(c_d)log(n), where constant c_d is specifically calculated for each depth value. Our results for depths 5 through 12 can be seen in a provided table, and we also derive general formulas for comparison networks, including those used in multi-way merging, which are essential components in binary searching networks. These findings contribute to a deeper understanding of the complexities of arrangement networks and may have far-reaching consequences for the design of efficient hash tables.

We employ a 1+1+2 covariant approach to describe a stellar object that exhibits anisotropic properties and dual-fluid characteristics within the framework of General Relativity, and we derive the corresponding Tolman-Oppenheimer-Volkoff equations in this context, which depend on three distinct parameters. The surface conditions for such a stellar body are previously established, and we provide specific examples, including one that avoids the formation of singularities even at the stellar surface, as well as another that replicates observations made for the Crab pulsar, and we derive the mass function, outgoing light rays, and redshift values, and we attempt to fit these results to observations, which yield reasonable outcomes, and we calculate the speed of sound, and we discover that anisotropic effects contribute positively to maintaining stability, and we conclude that dual-fluid systems may very well exist within the stellar realm.

Using observed properties of the Milky Way, we employ semi-analytical methods to study galaxy spiral structures, resulting in a sample of six simulated galaxies. By applying a mass-composite technique, we create stellar orbits that replicate observed GISX and COBE maps, yielding final galaxy models. We derive relationships between spiral structure parameters and global galaxy properties, particularly those of dominant mass components. The relationship between stellar stream width and galaxy mass reveals a trend of increasing stream width with greater galaxy mass. Calculated pitch angles for inner and outer galaxy regions show a tendency for sharper angles in higher mass galaxies, while pattern speeds of four selected galaxies align with observed values when using the stellar mass within three effective radii as a reference.

Galactic mergers significantly shape galaxy evolution, especially during major mergers where galaxies combine to form larger entities. This study conducts sixteen high-resolution, heavy neutron star simulations that incorporate magnetic fields along with hydrodynamics, allowing for the examination of magnetic fields' effects on merging galaxy dynamics. These simulations resolute images at a subparseck scale, revealing the complex interactions between magnetic fields and gas within the galaxies, affecting their movement and eventual formation.

Identifying severe COVID-19 cases is essential for effective infection control and treatment, but it's a challenging task due to limited severe cases in datasets and vague symptom manifestations. To address this problem, we propose a novel approach called IAMNet, which combines contrastive learning and classification. Our method calculates the distance between augmented versions of images from normal, severe, and mild patients to prevent data augmentation from distorting symptom features and to capture infection-related representations. Experimental results on the COVID-19 CT dataset demonstrate that our model outperforms existing methods even under severe resource constraints. Additionally, our model's output visualizations and physician consultations reveal that it focuses on infected lung areas, indicating improved interpretability.

Most current sequence-to-sequence based error correction models rely on extensive data from multiple domains. In contrast, our research centers on enhancing model performance using limited data from new, unseen domains. We employ a meta-learning approach, fine-tuning models on several domains that share similar linguistic characteristics. Specifically, we adapt the multi-task graph convolution network with extra attention mechanisms and a graph-based decoder to facilitate error correction. Our method enables accurate error correction in new domains requiring only a small dataset, as we demonstrate with the Mentha dataset. Experimental results show our technique achieves superior performance over baseline methods, reducing the necessity for extensive error correction training data.

When analyzing financial/anatomical survey data, or census data, it's common to derive total counts from individually rounded numerical values. Due to prior rounding, ambiguity arises in determining the precise values of those numbers, thus creating a range of feasible potential counts. An investigation was conducted into the structure of this range of potential counts, as well as the development of methods to analytically assess the frequencies of each feasible potential count. Furthermore, formulas were created to calculate the most likely potential counts, along with the standard deviation of those potential counts. These formulations can also be used to develop efficient sampling techniques for more complex scenarios.

Researchers investigated the magnetic properties of GdInO$_3$ using bulk samples, with X-ray diffraction confirming a cation arrangement of Gd$^{3+}$ in the rhombohedral R-3c structure. Despite Gd$^{3+}$ having an ion configuration of $4f^7$ and $L$ = 0, which eliminates crystal electric field effects, slight deviations from this were observed at low temperatures, likely due to Gd$^{3+}$ sitting in off-center positions within the crystal lattice. As a result, an effective orbital moment could develop, influencing the material's low-temperature magnetic behavior as seen in neutron diffraction, ac susceptibility, and magnetization studies. Additionally, bulk GdInO$_3$ exhibited antiferromagnetic ordering at TN** = 1.61(2) K**, with two distinct magnetic transitions indicating Gd ion moments arranged in a triangular helical pattern in the basal plane and along the crystallographic c-axis.

We investigate the connection between self-interested behavior and fairness in scenarios where items must be allocated among agents, and no partial allocations are feasible. Allocations are subject to specification by a given system, which ensures fairness and influences an agent's decision-making process. We focus on the question of whether every allocation that maximizes social welfare represents a stable state, and answer it through an application to the distribution of identical items. Investigating a setting where items differ in value to each agent, and an allocation optimizes the sum of square roots of valuations, it turns out that all socially efficient allocations correspond to pure Nash equilibria, and only fair allocations are capable of representing social optimality.

In the domain of computer vision, adversarial training is a prevalent technique for unsupervised domain adaptation. Nevertheless, existing methods are limited to employing a one-to-one mapping under the supervised setting. Building upon this, we investigate the application of stochastic domain adaptation learning within the unsupervised context. Our research reveals that introducing randomness into the domain adaptation label technique yields enhanced performance improvements, surpassing traditional deterministic domain adaptation labels. Furthermore, we present a novel framework for stochastic domain adaptation labeling based on an energy minimization unit and a GAN. This innovative approach enables us to determine optimal stochastic labels both in the source and target domains. Without any network modifications, our proposed method seamlessly integrates with any UDA method. We provide theoretical support for this technique and present our results on several computer vision tasks, including image super-resolution, low-light enhancement, and generalization across datasets for pedestrian detection and pose estimation. Our work is limited to any UDA method and demonstrates significant performance gains in these tasks.

UGC 8839, an extremely faint spiral galaxy, exhibits unusual characteristics. It has minimal globular clusters, a substantial population of old stellar remnants in its disk, and a disproportionately high number of stars in its disk compared to its bulge. Furthermore, prior research focused predominantly on its disk and remnant system. However, a comprehensive analysis comparing mass distributions across spheres, disks, and halos reveals new insights. UC 8839's density profile in the half-radius between 0.16 to 0.76 kpc identifies a highly stable, compact disk. Its properties, including surface density, rotational velocity, and stability ratio, are rare even in the most stable galaxies. This discovery in UC 8839 represents the first instance of its kind at this radius.

Using paleo-detectors, which are massive scintillating detectors linked to present-day experiments like Super-Kamiokande, offers an excellent opportunity to improve limits on dark matter since they already account for neutrino backgrounds and have been verified. By taking advantage of paleo-detectors' million-ton detection mass equivalent, we can significantly reduce the minimum detectable dark matter mass to as low as 10 GeV, especially with improved sensitivity and better time frames. With a 10-year detection time and a detection mass of 10^9 kg, the neutrino floor will be reached for dark matter masses above 100 GeV, contributing to significant searches for dark matter.

This paper introduces a novel protocol called DP-Sync to safeguard modern synchronized databases, like Facebook Login, from phishing attacks. The protocol ensures that updates made to a client device are kept confidential from the server by leveraging the databases' sync features. To achieve this, DP-Sync incorporates differential privacy into the update process, modifying how data is encrypted and managing encryption keys. As a result, the protocol limits the amount of information the server can access, providing them with only approximate encryption patterns. Furthermore, DP-Sync allows for the recovery of accurate plaintext data, even after a client device has been compromised.

The effectiveness of machine learning models in security applications is largely dependent on their ability to generalize, which can be compromised by adversarial inputs. To address this challenge, our research focuses on providing a comprehensive assessment of feature significance within Random Forest models through a union bound method and mitigating overfitting-induced biases. By utilizing feature importance metrics and conducting error distribution examinations, we evaluate the influence of individual features on model predictions. Furthermore, our study introduces a modified Union Bound Criterion (MUB) to more accurately measure feature significance. The validity of MUB is confirmed through iterative adaption and adversarial analysis. MUB exhibits enhanced stability among tree iterations and demonstrates robustness against misclassification-induced feature significance distortion. Additionally, we introduce a new evaluation indicator, the MUC, to account for the relationship between randomness and significance. The MUC successfully identifies critical samples, facilitating the development of more resilient learning models.

Minimally invasive surgery has been greatly enhanced by image analysis technologies, particularly in identifying surgical instruments. These instruments are critical to understanding the overall scene and subsequently improving other complex tasks. Although there have been significant accomplishments in this field, current methods still face challenges when dealing with scenarios involving multiple instruments, limited visibility, or the need for precise real-time performance. This paper presents a novel approach to achieving highly accurate surgical instrument segmentation within the constrained environment of laparoscopic video. Our method utilizes a single network with an innovative, composite loss function that facilitates training on limited annotated data. It has been demonstrated on public datasets, and our model has shown promising results, outperforming state-of-the-art methods in terms of speed and accuracy.

Creating large-scale re-identification (re-id) datasets is laborious and expensive, thus unsupervised multi-pixel image classification (person) is frequently evaluated on public datasets with known identities. However, public datasets are limited in both scope and resolution compared to the requirements for traffic management systems. We introduce a groundbreaking framework that employs contrastive learning to train a low-cost, unsupervised individual re-identification model. This model can accurately distinguish between people and vehicles, and can be trained on a single dataset that contains only a single image per object. We successfully evaluated our model by re-identifying individuals on the Peking Road dataset, a challenging task that involves a vast array of objects and requires the system to process a large number of candidates.

This paper presents a novel high-frequency threshold assessment GARCH model and a corresponding framework that leverages lower tail dependence to forecast extreme market events. Our framework employs a latent variable approach and a non-parametric method to account for changes in the intraday threshold due to market conditions. It automatically adjusts the threshold as necessary, providing greater flexibility and adaptability, which is essential for accurately forecasting market extremes. Our analysis, based on S&P 500 futures, demonstrates the advantage of our approach over a standard threshold assessment GARCH model and alternative risk measurement methods, according to rigorous evaluation criteria including mean absolute error, root mean square error, and Theil's inequality coefficient.

Evaluating the stability of a telescope's imaging equipment is crucial for understanding the instrumental noise in the observed data. Typically, celestial objects like stars and planets are assumed to be free of intrinsic variability when used for this purpose, but this assumption is questionable in the case of radio pulsars. Although these objects exhibit a steady signal, they can still experience changes in brightness that are not uniform across the population, and this variability seems to be linked to their average brightness. Furthermore, studying the electronic system of a telescope can be significantly facilitated by analyzing the statistical properties of the scatter in pulsar timing data, an approach that has already been used for this purpose.

To determine associativity between two currents, a specific function is employed that measures the minimal energy required to excite a pair of charges at given spatial positions and minimizes the required energy. Based on this definition, a thorough investigation is carried out to establish the relationship between the association length and a particular coupling constant in quantum chromodynamics-like theories, as well as its implications for hadronic properties. A specific application is explored to understand how the association length between the up-quark and the anti-up-quark within a pion varies with the quark's spin configuration, providing a means to investigate the quark distribution within the pion.

Evaluating protoplanetary disk populations is affected by a range of uncertainties.
One key factor is the significant spread in measured values of key quantities.
Another important aspect is our incomplete understanding of how variables change over time.
Previous research indicates that traits such as optical/infrared excess and jet activity are linked to specific protoplanetary disk states.
However, there are also studies suggesting that the duration of these active phases is relatively brief.
We identify the most dynamic system among known active Juvenile Planetary Objects as XX Cha.
We observe a large discrepancy in the estimated accretion rate values for this object, with differences of up to five orders of magnitude possible.
This significant spread in rates is primarily attributed to the highly fluctuating nature of XX Cha's accretion process.
As a result, average accretion rate measurements can be significantly affected.
We propose that similar results may also apply to other objects with high activity levels.

We demonstrate a subtle inequality in resources that favor the less fortunate, which we term "inequality of chance." This phenomenon arises when considering the resources available to individuals or households within their specific socioeconomic circumstances. We developed an appropriate metric to quantify inequality of chance, and applied it to examine income redistribution among neighbors. Our research reveals that mild neighborly income redistribution can actually increase overall inequality of chance.

Consider a group G, which is derived from a linear algebraic group over a field, and let's denote its Galois group as $\Gamma$. The object of study involves Borel subalgebras, specifically their orbits under the action of the Galois group within a flag manifold, and various types of bannertypes can be used to classify these orbits. In this study, we've K-theoretically characterised the local rings of the rings of invariants for the inductive limit of Borel subalgebras, under the action of GL, and their Galois group equivalents, n-Borel algebras, n-Borel action flag manifolds, and their ring of invariants subalgebras.

The widespread adoption of machine learning has depended on high-quality data for nearly two decades. However, with ever-faster model advancement, progress in automatic data selection and cleaning has had to suffice with rule-based methods and heuristics that focus primarily on individual model performance. In contrast, modern machine learning systems typically employ end-to-end pipelines that encompass multiple components, including data preprocessing and model training, making it challenging to assess the impact of dataset issues on overall system output. This paper introduces DataDebug, a framework that utilizes Shapley values to analyze feature and data point importance within these comprehensive pipelines, enabling more precise data debugging within a game-theoretic setting.

This study explores the connection between radio emissions and dynamical interactions in a sample of galactic globular clusters by analyzing 116 galaxies across various ages and nuclear activities. Using a novel algorithm and the MAVERIC package, we identified 17 radio sources. We observe more radio emissions in older clusters and those with lower nuclear activity frequencies. Although no clear relationship exists between radio source intensity and central concentration, a correlation is found with horizontal half-radius. We classify 15 of the radio sources as extrinsic, originating from millisecond pulsars or low-mass X-ray binaries, and speculate that magnetic field interactions may exist within some low-mass binaries. Additionally, we propose 3 potential intrinsic sources, potentially associated with plasma processes similar to those occurring in active galactic nuclei. We detect more than twice the predicted number of sources, which can be attributed to underestimation in previous radio background predictions. A algorithm we developed is demonstrated to be a valuable tool for identifying unusual radio emissions in globular clusters.

We propose a novel method for reconstructing corrupted images using hypergraphs,
which addresses limitations of traditional graphs. Due to the high information
capacity of hyperedges, they're particularly effective for tasks like image
reconstruction, but difficult to work with directly. Our innovation lies in
transforming the hypergraph into a normal graph through 'shrinkage', enabling the
use of established regularization techniques based on adjacency matrices. Despite
this transformation, our method maintains a hypergraph loss function, guiding the
optimization process and preserving the original hypergraph's characteristics. We
developed the Guided Hypergraph Reconstruction method, which leverages these
elements to achieve accurate image recovery. Experimental results demonstrate the
superior performance of our approach in comparing it with state-of-the-art
alternatives.

We employ an entropic measure to determine when a light source within a microcavity emits directionally, by calculating changes in photon number fluctuations. Our approach overcomes limitations of previous methods, which were only applicable to systems adhering to specific statistical distributions. We also demonstrate that a significant drop in entropy in the photon number fluctuations indicates directional emission, and this criterion outperforms similar measures of distribution asymmetry. Our findings reveal that our threshold for directional emission correlates well with a recognized critical value and, moreover, we establish that entropic variations in emission patterns are directly related to the underlying physics of lasing, as opposed to other measures which may arise from minor system discrepancies.

We examine thermal atomic photons collected under a lens, revealing that their collective behavior mimics a quantum mechanical atom, producing a quantum interference effect known as the Mollow triplet in photon statistics. Our theoretical model incorporates thermal noise and perfectively describes both quantum and thermal contributions to photons. Furthermore, we propose an experimental verification using ultracold rubidium atoms, and utilize microscopic molecular photons for precise testing, finding excellent agreement in our results.

Offline learning for multiple interacting agents is significantly harder than single-agent learning due to the challenges of estimating both the environment and how agents interact with one another from observed data. Due to data scarcity, researchers often collect interactions from all users, which can then be utilized to train every individual agent. However, this approach leads to a phenomenon known as the behavioral externalities problem, which hampers standard offline learning methods. To overcome this problem, our proposed framework, called Good Path Learning (GOLER), enables the simultaneous estimation of the environment and agent policies from data that may lack high quality. By introducing a generalization of offline reinforcement learning into an agent's utility function, we can modify the data collection process to include implicit comparisons between the best and least effective possible agent actions, which, according to our generalization, yields more informative state-based statistics. By leveraging GoleraNet, a neural network that models agents' utility functions and incorporates these implicit interactions, we can achieve superior results in terms of sample efficiency, stability, and overall performance.

Due to improved patient positioning accuracy, MV image registration with kilovoltage images is now a common practice in radiotherapy treatment, allowing for real-time beam intensity modulation. As an option for 3D image generation from multiple MV images, super-resolution presents itself as a suitable technique with certain advantages, including reduced noise and a lack of geometric distortion. However, direct upscaling methods tend to fall short in producing distorted and unreliable results. This research explores employing convolutional neural networks for mapping low-resolution 2D MV images to high-resolution 3D CT images and compares two training strategies: direct scaling from 2D to 3D images, or initial linear interpolation to an intermediate resolution followed by direct scaling. Results indicate a notable improvement in registration metrics and visual quality.

We investigate single-particle steering, a phenomenon where the existence of one particle influences the existence of another distant particle. To demonstrate single-particle steering effectively, we establish both necessary and sufficient conditions. Furthermore, we show that it defies a local hidden variable framework, implying that one can ascertain nonlocal information about a system. Notably, we show that single-particle entanglement resources are what make this possible.

The integration of Artificial Intelligence techniques and the Federation of Learning within the Internet of Vehicles is set to accelerate, but this advancement also brings an increased risk of security breaches and privacy violations. Utilizing the Blockchain technology within an FL framework can help mitigate these threats by providing enhanced security, privacy protection, and transparency within the FL framework within the Internet of Vehicles. Within this review, we provide a comprehensive analysis of existing research proposals within the Blockchain-FL framework within the Internet of Vehicles. Furthermore, we explore the primary applications of this technology within the areas of provide enhanced security, privacy protection, and transparency within the FL framework within the Internet of Vehicles. Within this review, we provide a detailed examination of the security threats that loom over this Blockchain-FL framework, including an investigation of its current usability within the Internet of Vehicles. Within this research, key challenges that hinder the progression of this Blockchain-FL framework, including an increase in computational complexity, reduced system efficiency, and scarcity of suitable blockchain technologies, are identified. Within this review, we provide a forward-looking perspective on Blockchain-FL framework within the Internet of Vehicles, including an investigation of its potential development, including an examination of its performance, the influence of blockchain technologies, and the importance of privacy within the FL framework within the Internet of Vehicles.

V392 Persei, a well-known dwarf nova that underwent a classic nova explosion in 2018, is now established as an exceptional object.  V392 Per is an extremely low mass white dwarf, with only 0.49 times the mass of the Sun, which is 0.84 times the size of the Sun, and spins at an incredible 2.5 times per second.  V392 Per is now known to emit X-rays with extreme brightness, with its X-ray luminosity reaching 10^31 times the power of the Sun, and also shows faint gamma-ray emissions in its spectrum.  V392 Per now has an estimated mass for its companion star of 0.33 times the mass of the Sun, with its gamma-ray and X-ray emissions well-modeled by a classic magnetic star-eating model of novae, with its magnetic field being 35 million times stronger than that of the Earth.  However, V392 Per is an unusual object because it has both gamma-ray and X-ray emissions, which is rare for magnetic DW Novae, and because its spin period has dramatically slowed since its 2018 eruption.  V392 Per is now observed to emit lines of sulfur in its optical spectrum, with its spectrum also filled with hydrogen and ionized helium. In quantum computing, combining multiple qubits into entangled states is an essential skill. Investigating the disparity between two-qubit and multi-qubit gate operations within the toric code, we found that comparing these operations necessitates state states with equivalent error protection capabilities. As qubit count increases in a multi-qubit gate, the level of error protection provided by the code's logical space remains constant. Calculations show that while two-qubit operations require around 43 physical qubits to achieve a certain level of error protection, their constant-qubit-count nature makes them more efficient than their multi-qubit counterparts, which could be important in designing more effective quantum error correction techniques.

This research proposes a precoder codebook and feedback encoding method tailored for the research and development of a 5G mobile network, addressing the limitations of 4G systems. The study focuses on enhancing wideband channel performance, rather than local peaks, by developing and optimizing pre-coded filters to adapt to user requirements and hardware constraints. A codebook structure comprising optimized filters and Gaussian mixture model densities is proposed, allowing for efficient codebook search within limited feedback conditions. The proposed method reduces codebook search requirements by representing the5G system's complexities within this structure. The research develops an algorithm to find the optimal pre-coded filters and codebook size within limited feedback conditions, and demonstrates its effectiveness through numerical results.

In a 2D system, a steady current that flows along the boundary occurs under certain conditions of disordered magnetic fields and is preserved under some perturbations, phenomenon known as the Hall effect, which takes place without the need for an external magnetic field. Now, we discovered the analogous effect in a 3D system, which arises in the 3D Hofstadter model and is found in a lattice system that supports nonequilibrium chiral modes, which are robust and operate independently of an external magnetic field. A key property of this system is its robust isolation of the surface layers into two 2D platforms, where these currents are found and are analogous to the Hall effect, occurring without the need for an external magnetic field.

The mass that stars lose through radiation, wind, and the dynamics of gas 
collection is fundamentally linked to the mass they possess. This relationship 
can be understood by examining the mass a star acquires through gravitational 
attraction, specifically the mass that is funneled towards it. 
Researching systems that utilize the Bondi mechanism to acquire mass, such as 
binary systems and black holes at the center of galaxies, provides a 
counterpart to analyzing systems driven by wind forces. 
To illustrate this concept, a solar-like star in a one-solar radius orbit around 
a central black hole, with a period of 3 hours, is investigated. 
Although most of the mass that is attracted to the star is still accreted by it, 
at least 10 percent reaches the black hole even when there is no accretion 
occuring on the star. 
While this is the case for systems consisting of compact objects and white 
dwarfs, a greater threshold of 100 kilometers is required for a star to overcome 
a black hole in a comparable orbit.

We investigate the impact of nuclear star clusters on the formation of Population III binaries in massive zapping galaxies by transferring the core cores of such systems. Core-halo configurations arise from active star formation in the main galaxy, with Pop III cores residing within zapping spheres of normal stars. The dynamic environment of nuclear clusters significantly affects Pop III's evolution, often causing collisions with normal stars and tidal disruptions within a short cosmic time. Considering structure formation models that include Pop III cores within zapping spheres, we determine that such systems have a much lower probability of retaining supermassive black holes formed from Pop III binaries. In contrast, isolated Pop III systems are more likely to produce such black holes. As most very high redshift Lyman-break galaxies are associated with galaxies, nuclear clusters reduces the predicted BH merger rate in a manner consistent with LIGO-Virgo observations.
